one_liner: Stable branchless quicksort/mergesort hybrid with a qsort-style C interface, claimed ~3x faster than std::stable_sort on random ints.
what_it_does: Fluxsort is a general-purpose stable sort for arrays, offered as a drop-in alternative to qsort/std::stable_sort rather than a C++ template. It exposes the standard C qsort(3) signature (array, nmemb, size, cmp) for arbitrary types, plus fluxsort_prim(array, nmemb, size) for primitive 32/64-bit signed or unsigned integers with no comparator needed, and fluxsort_size(array, nmemb, size, cmp) for a by-reference comparator on any element size.
how_it_is_fast: A top-down analyzer first checks for fully ordered/reversed runs and per-quarter presortedness, falling back to its sibling quadsort when a segment is mostly ordered. Partitioning is quicksort-style but partially in-place: elements <=pivot are written back in place and elements >pivot go to an auxiliary swap buffer, which cuts the branch-misprediction cost that plagues classic quicksort and gives memory-level parallelism on the writes. Pivots are chosen via a branchless quasimedian-of-9 (up to a median of 1024 for large partitions, an approximation of cbrt(n)), and partitions under 96 elements are sorted with quadsort's branchless small-array routine; a 1/16 partition-imbalance guard bounds the worst case to n log n.
when_to_use: Stable sorting of primitive fixed-width integers, longs, or doubles (8/16/32/64-bit, long double) where you would otherwise use std::stable_sort
Arrays from ~10K to 10M elements of random or partially-ordered data on x86-64/GCC, where extra O(n) scratch memory is affordable
Data with exploitable structure - ascending/descending runs, sawtooth, pipe-organ patterns - where the analyzer gives the largest (10-18x) gains
C/C++ code that can vendor a small C source drop and compile it with GCC -O3 (the author's tuned toolchain)
Offline/batch sorting where a first-party-benchmarked throughput gain is sufficient evidence, not latency-critical or safety-certified code
when_not_to_use: You need the actual std::stable_sort C++ template API (iterators, allocators, arbitrary value types by move) - fluxsort is a C function with the qsort comparator contract, a code change, not a header swap

Memory is constrained: fluxsort allocates n elements of swap memory (shared with quadsort); if allocation fails it silently falls back to quadsort's slower in-place rotations. Use blitsort (same author) for a true in-place stable sort

Your comparator is subtraction-based (`a - b`) or otherwise not a strict, overflow-safe ordering - reported "bugs" (issue #10 buffer overflow, issue #4 stability failure) both turned out to be caller comparator mistakes, but they show how easy this footgun is to hit

You need current, independently verified performance evidence: the project is stale (last commit 2024-07-27) and every published benchmark is first-party (author's own bench.c/wolfsort suite) on an old GCC 7.5.0/WSL toolchain with hardware unstated

You're sorting only unsigned 32-bit ints at very large scale and can use radix sorting instead - the README itself says wolfsort (adaptive radix, same author) beats fluxsort on 8/16/32-bit types, and crumsort beats it if stability isn't required

integration.dependencies: none (fluxsort.h textually includes fluxsort.c and bundles quadsort.h/quadsort.c for the small-array/run fallback; all four files must sit in the same directory)
integration.min_toolchain: Plain C (no version stated beyond needing stdlib.h/string.h/assert.h); author recommends compiling with gcc -O3 for the numbers claimed - the README's own clang-10 benchmark shows some fluxsort/quadsort routines 2-3x slower under clang
integration.platforms: any (portable C, no SIMD/intrinsics in the header); all published benchmarks are x86-64 (WSL/Ubuntu)
integration.thread_safety: not documented - no shared/global state visible in fluxsort.h beyond per-call swap allocation, but concurrent use is never discussed
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: matches C qsort(3)'s (array, nmemb, size, cmp) shape, not std::stable_sort's C++ template signature, so callers must switch call sites, not just link a different library

gotchas: Comparator must be a real strict ordering that returns a consistent sign for all inputs; `a - b`-style comparators on 64-bit values silently truncate/overflow to int and cause out-of-bounds writes or unstable results (reported as a fluxsort bug in issue #10, root-caused to the caller's comparator)

fluxsort_prim only covers 32/64-bit signed/unsigned integers (size = sizeof(int) or sizeof(long long), +1 to select unsigned); anything else needs fluxsort_size with a by-reference comparator, same as sorting an array of pointers
Falls back silently to quadsort (still stable, but in-place via rotations) if the swap-memory malloc fails - a correctness safety net that is also a silent performance cliff

A closed 2024 issue shows a Rust-glue port mismapped its comparator into fluxsort's internal contract and produced an apparent stability failure; the C library itself is not the source of that bug, but it illustrates how fragile porting the comparator convention is
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick fluxsort over the unstable/radix/SIMD siblings (BlockQuicksort, IPS4o, x86-simd-sort, LearnedSort, poor-circle/radix_sort) when you need a stable, portable scalar C sort rather than raw unsigned-int throughput. Prefer quadsort itself, its stablemate, when the data has long ordered runs or is strings/objects (README: quadsort's branchless merge beats fluxsort there); fluxsort's edge is random or low-cardinality data plus the same qsort-style interface.
verified_claims_summary: Author's own bench.c (wolfsort benchmark suite), compiled with g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive on GCC 7.5.0/Ubuntu 18.04 under WSL, hardware unstated: best-of-100 sorting 100,000 random 32-bit ints took 0.001906s for fluxsort vs 0.006113s for std::stable_sort (~3.2x); on ascending-order input, 0.000044s vs 0.000804s (~18x); 64-bit random ints were 0.002032s vs 0.006008s (~3.0x).
status_note: Stale (last commit 2024-07-27) but Unlicense (public-domain) makes it safe to freeze and vendor; the only known-good configuration is the author's GCC 7.5.0 -O3 toolchain, and no independent benchmark against std::stable_sort was found.
